blocks.md:
English needs a separate word: *I **am** a student*. Korean does not. The ending goes **onto the noun itself**.

저는 학생**이에요**. / I am a student.

blocks.h: Which ending? Look at the last letter of the noun
blocks.md:
If the noun ends in a **consonant** (a 받침), use **-이에요**.
If it ends in a **vowel**, use **-예요**.
You will meet this shape again and again: **the form with the extra 이 goes after a consonant.** 이에요/예요 · 이/가 · 은/는 · 을/를 all split the same way. Get the feel once here and the rest come almost free.

items.tip: I am Korean. 사람 ends in ㅁ, a consonant → 이에요
My friend is a doctor. 의사 ends in ㅏ, a vowel → 예요

blocks.q: Only one of these follows the rule. Which?
blocks.why: 커피 ends in the vowel ㅣ → **예요**. The other three break the rule: 의사 and 가수 end in vowels so they need **예요**, and 선생님 ends in ㅁ so it needs **이에요**.
학생 ends in ㅇ, a consonant, so it takes the longer **이에요**.

blocks.meaning: My younger sibling is a singer.
blocks.why: 가수 ends in the vowel ㅜ, so the 이 drops and you get **예요**.
커피 ends in ㅣ, a vowel → **예요**.

blocks.q: Which noun would take **-이에요**?
blocks.why: 사람 ends in ㅁ, a consonant → 사람**이에요**. 의사, 가수 and 커피 all end in vowels, so they take **예요**.

blocks.q: Match each noun with its ending.
“I am a teacher.”  저는 선생님___
Now write the whole sentence yourself: **“I am a student.”**
blocks.hint: Start with 저는. Then the noun with the right ending, 학생 ends in a consonant.
blocks.why: 저는 학생이에요. 전 is a shortened 저는 and is also fine in speech.

blocks.q: Say it out loud: “I am a student.”

blocks.md:
To say something is **not** so, you do not negate 이에요. You swap in a different word entirely: **아니에요**.

저는 학생이 **아니에요**. / I am not a student.

The noun before 아니에요 takes **이/가**, not 은/는.

저는 의사**가** 아니에요.  (○)
저는 의사**는** 아니에요.  (△, possible, but it means “*a doctor*, I am not, though maybe something else”)
Same split as yesterday: **이** after a consonant, **가** after a vowel. Notice 아니에요 itself never changes, only the particle in front of it does.

items.tip: I am not Japanese. 사람 + 이
This is not coffee. 커피 + 가
My friend is not a singer.

blocks.q: “이거는 물___ 아니에요.”  (물 = water, ends in ㄹ)
blocks.why: 아니에요 takes **이/가**, and 물 ends in a consonant → **물이**. 물은 is the topic particle and 물을 is the object particle, neither belongs in front of 아니에요.
아니에요 wants **이/가**, and 의사 ends in a vowel → **가**. **이** is the same particle for consonant-final nouns, **는** marks a topic, **를** marks an object.

blocks.q: Match each noun with the particle it takes before 아니에요.
Build “This is not coffee.”

blocks.meaning: My friend is not a singer.
blocks.why: 가수 ends in a vowel → **가**. **이** is for consonant-final nouns, **는** marks a topic, **도** means “also”.

blocks.q: Which sentence is built correctly?
blocks.why: 아니에요 takes **이/가**, and 사람 ends in ㅁ → 사람이 아니에요. 를 is the object tag; 안 이에요 tries to negate 이에요 with 안, which Korean does not do, the negative word is 아니에요.

blocks.q: Write it yourself: **“I am not a doctor.”**
blocks.hint: The noun before 아니에요 takes 이/가: and 의사 ends in a vowel.
blocks.why: 저는 의사가 아니에요. 의사**는** 아니에요 is possible too, but it adds a contrast, “*a doctor* I am not, though maybe something else.”

blocks.q: Say it out loud: “I am not a doctor.”

title.ko: 3강. 이름과 물건 소개하기: 이에요/예요 꼴 만들기
title.en: Lesson 3. Naming People & Things, Forming 이에요/예요

blocks.md:
Now that you know **-이에요** follows a consonant and **-예요** follows a vowel, let's practice with names, nationalities, and everyday objects.

Notice that Korean names ending in a consonant take **-이에요**, while names ending in a vowel take **-예요**.
When introducing yourself, you can say **저는 [Name]이에요/예요** or shorten **저는** to **전**: **전 민수예요** (I'm Minsu).

items.tip: I am American. 사람 ends in a consonant ㅁ → 이에요.
This person is my friend Sujin. 수진 ends in a consonant ㄴ → 이에요.
That (over there) is a bag. 가방 ends in a consonant ㅇ → 이에요.
This is a chair. 의자 ends in a vowel ㅏ → 예요.

blocks.q: Match each word to its correct ending form.
Choose the correct sentence to introduce Minji (민지).
blocks.why: 민지 ends in the vowel ㅣ, so it takes **-예요**. 민지이에요 breaks the vowel contraction rule.
책 ends in the consonant ㄱ (받침), so it attaches **-이에요** to become **책이에요**.

blocks.q: Complete the sentence with the correct form: “This is a desk (책상).” → 이거는 책상___
blocks.why: 책상 ends in the consonant ㅇ (받침), so it takes **-이에요**.

blocks.q: Assemble the sentence: “I am American.”
Say out loud: “I am Jihoon. Nice to meet you.”

title.en: Lesson 4. Sorting the Pair: 이에요/예요 vs. 아니에요

blocks.h: Affirmative vs. Negative: The Particle Trap
blocks.md:
Beginners often get confused by what comes *in front of* the ending:

1. **이에요 / 예요** attaches directly to the noun without any particle:
**학생이에요** (I am a student, NO particle!)

2. **아니에요** requires the subject particle **이/가**:
**학생이 아니에요** (I am not a student).

Never say *학생 안 이에요* or *학생을 아니에요*!
Remember: **이에요/예요** is a suffix glued to the noun. **아니에요** is an independent adjective word meaning 'to not be', which is why the noun before it needs the subject marker **이/가**.

items.tip: This is water. It is not alcohol. (물 + 이에요 / 술 + 이 아니에요)
I am not a teacher. I am a student. (선생님 + 이 아니에요 / 학생 + 이에요)
It's not my bag. It's my friend's bag.

blocks.q: Which sentence incorrectly adds a particle before 이에요?
blocks.why: 이에요/예요 attaches directly to the noun with **no particle**. Saying **학생이 이에요** is wrong; it should be simply **학생이에요**.

blocks.meaning: This is not juice. It is water.
blocks.why: 주스 ends in a vowel (ㅡ), so it takes **가 아니에요**. Korean never says *안 이에요*.

blocks.q: Match each affirmative sentence with its negative counterpart.
Arrange the words to say: “I am not a teacher. I am a student.”
Complete the sentence with the negative form of 의사: “저는 ___ .” (I am not a doctor.)
blocks.why: 의사 ends in a vowel, so it takes **가 아니에요**.

blocks.say: 저는 일본 사람이 아니에요. 한국 사람이에요.
blocks.rom: jeo-neun il-bon sa-ram-i a-ni-e-yo. han-guk sa-ram-i-e-yo.
blocks.q: Say out loud: “I am not Japanese. I am Korean.”
